newsitem.title: GERMANY: Talk of compromise in German sick pay dispute.
newsitem.headline: Talk of compromise in German sick pay dispute.

text.p: German engineering employers and workers on Thursday hinted they were ready to look at possible compromises as they prepared for more talks over controversial proposals to cut sick pay benefits.

Leaders of the IG Metall trade union, fresh from success in forcing employers to postpone implementing a law that cuts sick pay by 20 percent, said concessions elsewhere on labour costs were now possible.

Speaking ahead of talks in Frankfurt with the Gesamtmetall employers federation, IG Metall deputy chairman Walter Riester said the union would still seek a nationally-binding clause protecting sick pay at the current 100 percent of salary.
"That could also have a price for our side," Riester conceded in Thursday's Hamburger Abendblatt paper.

In contrast to last week's forceful rhetoric when more than 100,000 metal workers temporarily walked out in protest at the proposed cuts, other union leaders suggested certain out-of-date work regulations could now be revised to cut costs.

"We could also discuss some of those framework regulations that came into being 10 years ago but are possibly not valid today," Gerhard Zambelli, regional IG Metall union leader in the state of Baden-Wuerttemberg, told German television.

Zambelli, one of the key figures in last week's protests against Daimler-Benz AG's attempt to implement the law, repeated an earlier offer that sick pay could be based on basic pay rather than taking into account overtime payments.
Sick pay has previously been based on average total pay over an agreed period, including the the assumption that a worker would have continued to work overtime if he were not ill.

Zambelli calculated his proposal would have the same effect on costs as reducing sick pay to 80 percent of salary -- which employers estimate could cut as much as 12 billion marks ($7.84 billion) off annual labour costs.
Gesamtmetall president Werner Stumpfe, who initially advised federation members to implement the sick pay cuts immediately, echoed the more conciliatory tone taken by the unions.

"We must find a compromise that is a fair balance of interests through a true social partnership with the unions," Stumpfe said, using the vocabulary of consensus that had appeared to have been all but lost in this dispute.
Stumpfe rejected any general move to cut the average working week for metal workers, one possibility raised by unions this week as a way of securing jobs in the recession-hit industry.

IG Metall on Tuesday said it would settle for a 1997 wage increase in line with inflation as long as employers agreed to job protection policies aimed at stemming the flow of redundancies in the sector.

Gesamtmetall has said it would be ready to discuss such an inflation-based rise in 1997 wages but only if real cuts in labour costs could also be achieved -- a goal seemingly incompatible with the union's job protection demands. -- Frankfurt Newsroom + 49 69 756525 ($1=1.5315 Mark)
